chapters.title: Job and the Accuser
chapters.html:
Job 1

The Man from Uz

1There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job. That man was blameless and upright; he feared God and turned away from evil.

2Seven sons and three daughters were born to him.

3His livestock was seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen and five hundred female donkeys, with a great many servants; that man was the greatest of all the people of the east.

4His sons would go and hold a feast, in the house of each one on his day, and they would send and invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them.

5When the days of the feast had gone their round, Job would send and consecrate them. He would rise early in the morning and offer burnt offerings by the number of them all, for Job said, "Perhaps my sons have sinned and cursed God in their hearts." This is what Job did all the days.

The First Test

6And it came to pass one day that the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them.

7The LORD said to Satan, "Where have you come from?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From roaming over the earth and from walking about on it."

8The LORD said to Satan, "Have you set your heart on My servant Job? For there is no one like him on the earth, a man blameless and upright, who fears God and turns away from evil."

9Satan answered the LORD and said, "Is it for nothing that Job fears God?

10Have You not put a hedge around him and around his house and around all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his livestock has spread out over the land.

11But stretch out Your hand now and touch all that he has, and he will surely curse You to Your face."

12The LORD said to Satan, "All that he has is in your hand; only do not stretch out your hand against him." Satan went out from the presence of the LORD.

13And it came to pass one day, as his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their brother the firstborn,

14that a messenger came to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys grazing beside them,

15and Sheba fell on them and took them, and they struck the young men with the edge of the sword. I alone have escaped to tell you."

16While he was still speaking, another came and said, "The fire of God fell from heaven and burned up the sheep and the young men and consumed them. I alone have escaped to tell you."

17While he was still speaking, another came and said, "The Chaldeans formed three bands, raided the camels and took them, and they struck the young men with the edge of the sword. I alone have escaped to tell you."

18While he was still speaking, another came and said, "Your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their brother the firstborn,

19and suddenly a great wind came from across the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house. It fell on the young people, and they are dead. I alone have escaped to tell you."

Job's Answer

20Job rose, tore his robe and shaved his head; he fell to the ground and bowed down.

21He said,
"Naked I came out of my mother's womb,
and naked I will return there.
The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken;
blessed be the name of the LORD."

22In all this Job did not sin, nor did he charge God with wrong.

Notes

  • The text of Job — rendered from the Hebrew. The book is a story in prose (chapters 1–2 and 42:7–17) around a long debate in verse. The Greek translation of Job is shorter than the Hebrew, by about a sixth; where it differs in a way that matters, the note says so.

  • v1 "the land of Uz" — east of Israel, toward Edom (Lamentations 4:21). Blameless, tam, is whole, of one piece; God repeats all four of the narrator's words about Job in v8 and again in 2:3.

  • v5 and v11 "cursed God… curse You" — the Hebrew says berakhu, blessed. The scribes would not write "curse God," and put "bless" in its place; the sense is plain from the story. The same word returns at 2:5 and 2:9, and stands in its plain sense, "blessed," at 1:10 and 1:21.

  • v6 "the sons of God" — the members of God's heavenly court, as in 38:7. Satan is ha-satan, with the article, the accuser or the adversary: a title in this book, as in Zechariah 3:1–2, not yet a name.

  • v7 "roaming over the earth" — mi-shut, the verb of the eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth (Zechariah 4:10; 2 Chronicles 16:9).

  • v9 "Is it for nothing that Job fears God?" — ha-chinnam, for nothing, without cause: the question of the whole book. God answers with the same word in 2:3, you incited Me against him to destroy him without cause.

  • vv15–19 — the losses alternate between raiders and fire or wind from heaven: Sheba, from Arabia (6:19); the fire of God, lightning, as in 1 Kings 18:38 and 2 Kings 1:12; the Chaldeans, the people of Babylonia, here still raiders of the desert. Ha-ne'arim is the young men, the servants, in vv15–17; in v19 the same word means Job's own children, the young people.

  • v21 "Naked I came out of my mother's womb" — As he came from his mother's womb he shall go again, naked as he came (Ecclesiastes 5:15); we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out (1 Timothy 6:7). There is the earth, the mother of all (Psalm 139:15; Sirach 40:1).

  • v22 "nor did he charge God with wrong" — tiflah, what is unseemly, folly: he did not ascribe anything unfitting to God.

chapters.title: The Second Test
chapters.html:
Job 2

Skin for Skin

1And it came to pass one day that the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them to present himself before the LORD.

2The LORD said to Satan, "Where have you come from?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From roaming over the earth and from walking about on it."

3The LORD said to Satan, "Have you set your heart on My servant Job? For there is no one like him on the earth, a man blameless and upright, who fears God and turns away from evil. He still holds fast to his integrity, though you incited Me against him to swallow him up without cause."

4Satan answered the LORD and said, "Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life.

5But stretch out Your hand now and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will surely curse You to Your face."

6The LORD said to Satan, "He is in your hand; only keep his life."

7Satan went out from the presence of the LORD and struck Job with evil sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.

8He took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself with, as he sat among the ashes.

9His wife said to him, "Do you still hold fast to your integrity? Curse God and die."

10He said to her, "You speak as one of the foolish women speaks. Shall we receive good from God, and not receive evil?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips.

The Three Friends

11When Job's three friends heard of all this evil that had come on him, they came each from his own place, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite. They had agreed together to come to show him sympathy and to comfort him.

12When they lifted up their eyes from far off, they did not recognize him. They lifted up their voices and wept; each tore his robe, and they threw dust on their heads toward the sky.

13They sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his pain was very great.

Notes

  • vv1–3 — the scene of 1:6–8 told again in the same words, with one line added: He still holds fast to his integrity. Tummah, integrity, is the noun of tam, blameless, and Job's wife throws it back at him in v9.

  • v3 "without cause" — chinnam, the word of Satan's question in 1:9, Is it for nothing that Job fears God? The LORD now turns it back: the suffering was for nothing.

  • v4 "Skin for skin!" — a saying of trade, like-for-like: a man will give up any skin, any possession, to save his own.

  • v6 "only keep his life" — et nafsho shemor, guard his life: Satan may strike, but he must keep Job alive.

  • v7 "evil sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head" — shechin ra, the very curse of Deuteronomy 28:35, The LORD will strike you… with grievous boils of which you cannot be healed, from the sole of your foot to the crown of your head.

  • v9 "Curse God and die" — the Hebrew is barekh, bless, as at 1:5 and 1:11 and 2:5. The Greek gives Job's wife a longer speech here, telling of her own wanderings and labor since the losses; the Hebrew has only these words.

  • v10 "one of the foolish women" — nevalot, from naval, the fool who says in his heart, There is no God (Psalm 14:1); not a lack of brains but a lack of reverence.

  • v11 the three friends — Teman is in Edom, named for a grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:11); Is wisdom no more in Teman? (Jeremiah 49:7). Shuah was a son of Abraham by Keturah, sent east (Genesis 25:2, 6). Naamah is not otherwise known as a place.

  • v13 "seven days and seven nights" — the time of mourning for the dead; Joseph made a mourning for his father seven days (Genesis 50:10).

chapters.title: Job Curses His Day
chapters.html:
Job 3

1After this Job opened his mouth and cursed his day.

2Job answered and said:

Let the Day Perish

3Let the day perish on which I was born,
and the night that said, "A man is conceived."

4That day, let it be darkness;
let God above not seek it,
nor light shine on it.

5Let darkness and deep shadow claim it;
let a cloud settle on it;
let the blackness of the day terrify it.

6That night, let gloom seize it;
let it not rejoice among the days of the year;
let it not come into the number of the months.

7Let that night be barren;
let no shout of joy come into it.

8Let those who curse the day damn it,
those who are ready to rouse Leviathan.

9Let the stars of its twilight be dark;
let it wait for light, and have none,
and not see the eyelids of the dawn,

10because it did not shut the doors of my mother's womb,
nor hide trouble from my eyes.

Why Did I Not Die?

11Why did I not die from the womb,
come out from the belly and breathe my last?

12Why did knees receive me,
or why breasts, that I should nurse?

13For now I would have lain down and been quiet;
I would have slept; then I would be at rest,

14with kings and counselors of the earth,
who rebuilt ruins for themselves,

15or with princes who had gold,
who filled their houses with silver.

16Or like a hidden stillborn child I would not be,
like infants who never saw light.

17There the wicked cease from raging,
and there the weary of strength are at rest.

18The prisoners are at ease together;
they do not hear the voice of the taskmaster.

19The small and the great are there,
and the slave is free from his master.

Why Give Light?

20Why does He give light to the one in misery,
and life to the bitter of soul,

21who wait for death, and it does not come,
and dig for it more than for hidden treasure,

22who rejoice to the point of exulting,
and are glad when they find the grave?

23Why give light to a man whose way is hidden,
whom God has hedged in?

24For my sighing comes before my bread,
and my groans pour out like water.

25For the thing I feared has come on me,
and what I dreaded has come to me.

26I have no ease, I have no quiet, I have no rest,
and turmoil has come.

Notes

  • v1 "cursed his day" — qillel, the plain verb for cursing. Job does not curse God, as Satan said he would (1:11; 2:5), but the day of his birth. Cursed be the day on which I was born (Jeremiah 20:14–18).

  • v4 "let it be darkness" — yehi choshekh, the reverse of the first word of creation, yehi or, Let there be light (Genesis 1:3). God here is Eloah, the singular of Elohim, the name for God most used in the poetry of Job.

  • v5 "deep shadow" — tsalmavet, as in the valley of the shadow of death (Psalm 23:4).

  • v8 "those who curse the day… ready to rouse Leviathan" — those who were thought able to lay curses on days and to stir up the sea monster of chaos (41:1; Isaiah 27:1). With one letter changed, yom, day, would be yam, sea, the partner of Leviathan (7:12).

  • v10 "my mother's womb" — the Hebrew is bitni, my womb, the womb Job came from.

  • v14 "who rebuilt ruins for themselves" — kings who raised up ruined cities, or who built the great tombs that are now ruins; the phrase can bear both.

  • v16 "a hidden stillborn child" — nefel, as in it is better for the stillborn child than for him (Ecclesiastes 6:3).

  • v22 "to the point of exulting" — elei gil; with other vowels, elei gal, at the grave mound, which would match the second line.

  • v23 "whom God has hedged in" — the image of 1:10, where Satan said God had put a hedge around Job to protect him; now the hedge is a prison.

  • v26 "turmoil has come" — rogez, the raging of the wicked in v17 that ceases in the grave; for Job it has come in life.

chapters.title: Eliphaz Speaks
chapters.html:
Job 4

1Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:

You Have Strengthened Others

2If one tries a word with you, will you be weary?
Yet who can hold back from speaking?

3You have instructed many,
and you have strengthened weak hands.

4Your words have raised up the one who stumbled,
and you have made firm the knees that give way.

5But now it has come to you, and you are weary;
it touches you, and you are dismayed.

6Is not your fear of God your confidence,
and the blamelessness of your ways your hope?

7Remember now: who that was innocent ever perished?
Where were the upright cut off?

8As I have seen, those who plow iniquity
and sow trouble reap it.

9By the breath of God they perish,
and by the blast of His anger they are consumed.

10The roar of the lion, the voice of the fierce lion,
and the teeth of the young lions are broken.

11The lion perishes for lack of prey,
and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.

A Word in the Night

12A word came to me in secret,
and my ear caught a whisper of it.

13Among troubled thoughts from visions of the night,
when deep sleep falls on men,

14dread came on me, and trembling,
and made all my bones shake.

15A spirit glided past my face;
the hair of my flesh stood up.

16It stood still, but I could not make out its appearance;
a form was before my eyes;
there was silence, and I heard a voice:

17"Can mortal man be righteous before God?
Can a man be pure before his Maker?

18Even in His servants He puts no trust,
and His messengers He charges with error;

19how much more those who live in houses of clay,
whose foundation is in the dust,
who are crushed like the moth.

20Between morning and evening they are beaten to pieces;
with no one taking note, they perish forever.

21Is not their tent cord pulled up within them?
They die, and without wisdom."

Notes

  • v1 Eliphaz — the first of the three friends to speak, and the eldest, it seems (15:10). The debate runs in three rounds, each friend speaking in turn and Job answering each.

  • v6 "your confidence" — kislah, the trust a man rests on. Eliphaz begins gently: Job's own piety should be his hope.

  • v7 "who that was innocent ever perished?" — the friends' teaching in one line: the innocent do not perish, so the one who perishes cannot be innocent. I have not seen the righteous forsaken (Psalm 37:25).

  • v8 "those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap it" — Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity (Proverbs 22:8); whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Galatians 6:7).

  • vv10–11 the lions — five Hebrew words for lion in two verses (aryeh, shachal, kefir, layish, lavi): even the strongest of the wicked are broken.

  • v15 "A spirit glided past my face" — ruach, which can also be a breath of wind; the next verse shows a form standing before him.

  • v17 "righteous before God" — me-Eloah, which can also be read more righteous than God. The night voice's question returns in 9:2 and 25:4.

  • v18 "His messengers He charges with error" — mal'akhav, here the heavenly ones who serve Him. This book keeps messenger for mal'akh, as the rest of the Hebrew books do. He puts no trust in His holy ones (15:15).

  • v19 "houses of clay" — the body made from the dust (Genesis 2:7; 3:19); if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed (2 Corinthians 5:1).

  • v21 "their tent cord" — yitram, the cord that holds the tent up, pulled out and the tent collapses; the word can also mean their excellence, what remains of them.

chapters.title: Do Not Reject the Discipline
chapters.html:
Job 5

The Fool Taking Root

1Call now — is there anyone who will answer you?
To which of the holy ones will you turn?

2For vexation kills the fool,
and jealousy slays the simple.

3I have seen the fool taking root,
but suddenly I cursed his dwelling.

4His children are far from safety;
they are crushed in the gate, with no one to rescue them.

5The hungry eat his harvest,
and take it even from among the thorns,
and the snare gapes for their wealth.

6For trouble does not come out of the dust,
nor does misery sprout from the ground;

7but man is born to misery,
as the sparks fly upward.

I Would Seek God

8But as for me, I would seek God,
and to God I would commit my cause,

9who does great things beyond searching out,
wonders without number,

10who gives rain on the face of the earth
and sends water on the face of the fields,

11to set the lowly on high,
and those who mourn are lifted to safety.

12He frustrates the plans of the crafty,
so that their hands achieve no success.

13He catches the wise in their own craftiness,
and the counsel of the twisted is swept away.

14By day they meet darkness,
and grope at noon as in the night.

15But He saves the needy from the sword of their mouth,
and from the hand of the mighty.

16So the poor have hope,
and injustice shuts its mouth.

Blessed Is the One God Reproves

17Blessed is the man whom God reproves;
do not reject the discipline of the Almighty.

18For He wounds, and He binds up;
He strikes, and His hands heal.

19In six troubles He will deliver you;
in seven no evil will touch you.

20In famine He will redeem you from death,
and in war from the power of the sword.

21You will be hidden from the lash of the tongue,
and will not fear destruction when it comes.

22At destruction and hunger you will laugh,
and you will not fear the beasts of the earth.

23For you will have a covenant with the stones of the field,
and the beasts of the field will be at peace with you.

24You will know that your tent is at peace;
you will look over your fold and find nothing missing.

25You will know that your offspring are many,
and your descendants like the grass of the earth.

26You will come to the grave in ripe old age,
as a stack of sheaves goes up in its season.

27This we have searched out; so it is.
Hear it, and know it for yourself.

Notes

  • v1 "the holy ones" — the heavenly beings of God's court, the sons of God of 1:6 (15:15; Psalm 89:5–7). Eliphaz means that no one in heaven will take Job's side.

  • v5 "the snare gapes for their wealth" — tsammim, a snare; read with other vowels, tsme'im, the thirsty, as the Greek and Latin have it, matching the hungry of the first line.

  • v7 "as the sparks fly upward" — benei reshef, the sons of Resheph: flames, or birds, named after Resheph, the Canaanite god of fire and plague (Deuteronomy 32:24; Habakkuk 3:5).

  • vv9–10 — who does great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number returns on Job's own lips in 9:10.

  • v13 "He catches the wise in their own craftiness" — quoted by Paul in 1 Corinthians 3:19.

  • v17 "the Almighty" — Shaddai, the old name of God, used thirty-one times in Job, more than in all the rest of the Old Testament together. My son, do not despise the LORD's discipline (Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 12:5–6).

  • v18 "He wounds, and He binds up" — I wound and I heal (Deuteronomy 32:39); He has struck us down, and He will bind us up (Hosea 6:1).

  • v19 "In six troubles… in seven" — the counting pattern of wisdom sayings, six things the LORD hates, seven that are an abomination (Proverbs 6:16).

  • v24 "find nothing missing" — lo techeta, from chata, to miss the mark, the common verb for sin; here in its first sense.

  • v26 "a stack of sheaves goes up in its season" — the grain brought up to the threshing floor when it is ripe, not cut green.

speech.text: Job 5
The Fool Taking Root
Call now — is there anyone who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?
For vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple.
I have seen the fool taking root, but suddenly I cursed his dwelling.
His children are far from safety; they are crushed in the gate, with no one to rescue them.
The hungry eat his harvest, and take it even from among the thorns, and the snare gapes for their wealth.
For trouble does not come out of the dust, nor does misery sprout from the ground;
but man is born to misery, as the sparks fly upward.
I Would Seek God
But as for me, I would seek God, and to God I would commit my cause,
who does great things beyond searching out, wonders without number,
who gives rain on the face of the earth and sends water on the face of the fields,
to set the lowly on high, and those who mourn are lifted to safety.
He frustrates the plans of the crafty, so that their hands achieve no success.
He catches the wise in their own craftiness, and the counsel of the twisted is swept away.
By day they meet darkness, and grope at noon as in the night.
But He saves the needy from the sword of their mouth, and from the hand of the mighty.
So the poor have hope, and injustice shuts its mouth.
Blessed Is the One God Reproves
Blessed is the man whom God reproves; do not reject the discipline of the Almighty.
For He wounds, and He binds up; He strikes, and His hands heal.
In six troubles He will deliver you; in seven no evil will touch you.
In famine He will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword.
You will be hidden from the lash of the tongue, and will not fear destruction when it comes.
At destruction and hunger you will laugh, and you will not fear the beasts of the earth.
For you will have a covenant with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field will be at peace with you.
You will know that your tent is at peace; you will look over your fold and find nothing missing.
You will know that your offspring are many, and your descendants like the grass of the earth.
You will come to the grave in ripe old age, as a stack of sheaves goes up in its season.

chapters.title: My Brothers Like a Wadi
chapters.html:
Job 6

1Job answered and said:

Heavier than the Sand

2Oh that my vexation were weighed,
and my calamity laid with it in the scales!

3For now it would be heavier than the sand of the seas;
that is why my words have been rash.

4For the arrows of the Almighty are in me;
my spirit drinks their poison;
the terrors of God are arrayed against me.

5Does the wild donkey bray over its grass,
or the ox low over its fodder?

6Can what is tasteless be eaten without salt,
or is there any taste in the slime of the mallow?

7My soul refuses to touch them;
they are like sickness in my food.

8Oh that my request would come,
and that God would grant my hope,

9that God would be pleased to crush me,
that He would let loose His hand and cut me off!

10Then I would still have this comfort,
and would leap for joy in pain that does not spare,
for I have not denied the words of the Holy One.

11What is my strength, that I should wait?
What is my end, that I should be patient?

12Is my strength the strength of stones,
or is my flesh bronze?

13Is it not that there is no help in me,
and success has been driven from me?

Treacherous Friends

14The one who is fainting should have kindness from his friend,
even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty.

15My brothers have been treacherous like a wadi,
like the channels of wadis that pass away,

16which are dark with ice,
where the snow hides itself.

17When they are scorched, they vanish;
when it is hot, they are gone from their place.

18The caravans turn aside from their course;
they go up into the waste and perish.

19The caravans of Tema look,
the travelers of Sheba hope for them.

20They are ashamed because they trusted;
they come there and are put to shame.

21For now you have become like that;
you see a terror and are afraid.

22Have I said, "Give me something,"
or, "Offer a bribe for me from your wealth,"

23or, "Deliver me from the hand of the enemy,"
or, "Redeem me from the hand of the ruthless"?

24Teach me, and I will be silent;
make me understand how I have gone astray.

25How forceful are upright words!
But what does your reproof prove?

26Do you mean to reprove words,
when the speech of a despairing man is wind?

27You would even cast lots over the fatherless,
and bargain over your friend.

28But now be pleased to look at me;
I will not lie to your face.

29Turn back, please; let there be no injustice;
turn back, my righteousness is still at stake.

30Is there injustice on my tongue?
Cannot my palate tell what is ruinous?

Notes

  • v4 "the arrows of the Almighty" — God pictured as an archer, as in 16:12–13, He set me up as His target; His archers surround me; Your arrows have sunk into me (Psalm 38:2).

  • vv5–7 — the donkey and the ox do not complain when they have food; Job's complaint shows his food is the trouble. The slime of the mallow, rir challamut, is the juice of a plant, or by an old tradition the white of an egg; either way, tasteless.

  • v10 "the words of the Holy One" — Qadosh, a name for God used in Job only here. Job's comfort is that he has kept faith to the end.

  • v14 "The one who is fainting" — la-mas, a rare word; the sense of the line is uncertain, and it may also be read "whoever withholds kindness from his friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty."

  • vv15–20 "like a wadi" — a desert stream bed that runs full with snowmelt in winter and is dry in the heat, when travelers need it most.

  • v19 "Tema… Sheba" — oasis towns of Arabia on the caravan routes (Isaiah 21:14).

  • v21 "you have become like that" — the written text has lo, not: "you have become nothing"; the read form, followed here, has lo, to it: "you have become such," like the dry wadi.

  • v27 "cast lots over the fatherless" — gambling for a debtor's orphan as a slave (2 Kings 4:1; Joel 3:3).

  • v29 "turn back" — the written text has "my turning back" in the second line; the read form, followed here, repeats turn back.

chapters.title: What Is Man
chapters.html:
Job 7

Like a Hired Worker

1Is there not hard service for man on earth,
and are not his days like the days of a hired worker?

2Like a slave who longs for the shade,
and like a hired worker who waits for his wages,

3so I have been given months of emptiness,
and nights of misery are appointed to me.

4When I lie down I say, "When shall I rise?"
But the night is long, and I am full of tossing until the dawn.

5My flesh is clothed with worms and crusts of dust;
my skin hardens, then runs again.

6My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle;
they come to their end without hope.

7Remember that my life is a breath;
my eye will not again see good.

8The eye of the one who sees me will see me no more;
Your eyes will be on me, but I will be gone.

9As a cloud fades and goes,
so the one who goes down to Sheol does not come up.

10He does not return again to his house,
and his place does not know him anymore.

Am I the Sea?

11Therefore I will not hold back my mouth;
I will speak in the anguish of my spirit;
I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.

12Am I the sea, or the sea monster,
that You set a guard over me?

13When I say, "My bed will comfort me,
my couch will ease my complaint,"

14then You frighten me with dreams
and terrify me with visions,

15so that my soul would choose strangling,
death rather than these bones of mine.

16I despise it; I will not live forever.
Leave me alone, for my days are a breath.

17What is man, that You make so much of him,
that You set Your heart on him,

18visit him every morning
and test him every moment?

19How long will You not look away from me,
nor let me alone till I swallow my spit?

20If I have sinned, what do I do to You, watcher of mankind?
Why have You made me Your target,
so that I am a burden to myself?

21Why do You not pardon my transgression
and take away my iniquity?
For now I will lie down in the dust;
You will seek me, but I will not be.

Notes

  • v1 "hard service" — tsava, military service, a soldier's term of duty; Her warfare is ended (Isaiah 40:2).

  • v6 "swifter than a weaver's shuttle… without hope" — tiqvah, hope, is also thread (Joshua 2:18): the shuttle runs out of thread, and the days run out of hope.

  • v9 "Sheol" — the place of the dead, under the earth, from which no one comes back up (10:21–22).

  • v12 "the sea, or the sea monster" — yam and tannin, the powers of chaos that God holds in check (38:8–11; Psalm 74:13). Job asks whether he is so dangerous that God must keep him under guard.

  • v16 "I despise it" — ma'asti, with no object in the Hebrew; his life is meant. A breath, hevel, the word of Ecclesiastes, vanity of vanities.

  • vv17–18 "What is man, that You make so much of him?" — the words of Psalm 8:4, What is man that You are mindful of him? There the question wonders at God's care; here it begs to be left alone.

  • v19 "till I swallow my spit" — a saying for the shortest moment.

  • v20 "watcher of mankind" — notser ha-adam, the one who keeps watch over man; the word is used of God's care (Psalm 12:7), and Job feels it as a guard.

  • v20 "a burden to myself" — the Jewish scribes' tradition lists this among the places where they softened the text; it read a burden to You. The Greek has a burden to You.

  • v21 "You will seek me, but I will not be" — shichartani, seek me early, earnestly; God will come looking, and it will be too late.

chapters.title: Bildad Speaks
chapters.html:
Job 8

1Bildad the Shuhite answered and said:

Does God Pervert Justice?

2How long will you say these things,
and the words of your mouth be a mighty wind?

3Does God pervert justice,
or does the Almighty pervert what is right?

4If your children sinned against Him,
He has sent them away into the hand of their transgression.

5If you will seek God earnestly
and plead with the Almighty for mercy,

6if you are pure and upright,
surely then He will rouse Himself for you
and restore your rightful dwelling.

7Though your beginning was small,
your end will grow very great.

Ask the Former Generation

8For ask, please, of the former generation,
and set your mind to what their fathers searched out.

9For we are but of yesterday and know nothing,
for our days on earth are a shadow.

10Will they not teach you and tell you,
and bring out words from their heart?

11Can papyrus grow tall where there is no marsh?
Can reeds flourish without water?

12While it is still in flower, and not cut down,
it withers before any other grass.

13Such are the paths of all who forget God;
the hope of the godless will perish.

14His confidence is cut off,
and his trust is a spider's house.

15He leans on his house, but it does not stand;
he holds fast to it, but it does not last.

16He is green before the sun,
and his shoots spread over his garden.

17His roots twine around the stone heap;
he looks on a house of stones.

18If he is swallowed up from his place,
it will deny him: "I never saw you."

19That is the joy of his way,
and out of the dust others will spring up.

20God will not reject a blameless man,
nor take hold of the hand of evildoers.

21He will yet fill your mouth with laughter,
and your lips with shouts of joy.

22Those who hate you will be clothed with shame,
and the tent of the wicked will be no more.

Notes

  • v1 Bildad — the second friend. Where Eliphaz spoke of a vision (4:12–16), Bildad speaks from the tradition of the fathers (vv8–10).

  • v3 "Does God pervert justice?" — mishpat and tsedeq, justice and what is right, the two words Job will turn back on God (9:19–24; 19:7).

  • v4 "If your children sinned against Him" — Bildad says plainly what Eliphaz only hinted: Job's children died for their own sins. Compare Job's sacrifices for them in 1:5.

  • v6 "your rightful dwelling" — nevat tsidqekha, the pasture of your righteousness: the home that a righteous man deserves.

  • v7 "your end will grow very great" — the friend speaks better than he knows: the LORD blessed the latter days of Job more than his beginning (42:12).

  • v9 "we are but of yesterday" — our days on the earth are like a shadow (1 Chronicles 29:15).

  • vv11–12 papyrus and reeds — gome and achu, plants of the Nile marshes (Exodus 2:3; Genesis 41:2); without water they wither while still green.

  • v14 "His confidence is cut off" — yaqot, a word found only here; some read it as gossamer, a thread as frail as the spider's web in the next line.

  • vv16–19 — a second plant, flourishing in a garden and rooted among stones, then torn out so that even its place denies it.

  • v20 "a blameless man" — tam, the word of 1:1 for Job. Bildad holds out the promise on the condition he set in v6.

chapters.title: How Can a Man Be Right with God?
chapters.html:
Job 9

1Job answered and said:

The Power of God

2Truly I know that it is so;
but how can a man be in the right with God?

3If one wished to contend with Him,
he could not answer Him once in a thousand.

4He is wise in heart and mighty in strength;
who has hardened himself against Him and come out whole?

5He moves mountains, and they do not know it,
when He overturns them in His anger.

6He shakes the earth out of its place,
and its pillars tremble.

7He speaks to the sun, and it does not rise;
He seals up the stars.

8He alone stretches out the heavens
and treads on the back of the sea.

9He made the Bear and Orion,
the Pleiades and the chambers of the south.

10He does great things beyond searching out,
wonders without number.

11If He passes by me, I do not see Him;
He moves on, and I do not perceive Him.

12If He snatches away, who can turn Him back?
Who will say to Him, "What are You doing?"

13God does not turn back His anger;
beneath Him the helpers of Rahab bowed down.

No Arbiter Between Us

14How then can I answer Him,
choosing my words with Him?

15Though I am in the right, I cannot answer;
I must plead for mercy with my judge.

16If I called and He answered me,
I would not believe that He was listening to my voice.

17For He crushes me with a tempest
and multiplies my wounds without cause.

18He will not let me get my breath,
but fills me with bitter things.

19If it is a matter of strength, He is the mighty one!
If it is a matter of justice, who will summon me?

20Though I am in the right, my own mouth would condemn me;
though I am blameless, He would prove me crooked.

21I am blameless; I do not care about myself;
I despise my life.

22It is all one; therefore I say,
He destroys the blameless and the wicked.

23When the whip kills suddenly,
He mocks at the despair of the innocent.

24The earth is given into the hand of the wicked;
He covers the faces of its judges.
If not He, then who is it?

25My days are swifter than a runner;
they flee away; they see no good.

26They glide past like ships of reed,
like an eagle swooping on its prey.

27If I say, "I will forget my complaint,
I will put off my sad face and be cheerful,"

28I dread all my pains,
for I know You will not hold me innocent.

29I am to be condemned;
why then do I labor in vain?

30If I wash myself with snow
and cleanse my hands with lye,

31even then You will plunge me into a pit,
and my own clothes will abhor me.

32For He is not a man, as I am, that I might answer Him,
that we should come to trial together.

33There is no arbiter between us,
who might lay his hand on us both.

34Let Him take His rod away from me,
and let not dread of Him terrify me.

35Then I would speak without fear of Him,
for I am not so in myself.

Notes

  • v2 "how can a man be in the right with God?" — Job takes up the question of the night voice (4:17), but as a courtroom question: tsadaq, be in the right, win the case. The words of the law court run through the chapter: contend (v3), answer (vv14–16), judge (v15), summon (v19), condemn (v20), arbiter (v33).

  • v8 "treads on the back of the sea" — bamotei yam, the high places of the sea, as one treads on a defeated enemy; He walked on the sea (Mark 6:48–49).

  • v9 "the Bear and Orion, the Pleiades" — Ash, Kesil and Kimah, star groups named again in 38:31–32 and Amos 5:8; the identifications are traditional. The chambers of the south are the stars of the southern sky.

  • v10 — Job repeats Eliphaz's words of 5:9 almost exactly, but where Eliphaz praised God's power to help, Job fears it.

  • v13 "the helpers of Rahab" — Rahab is the sea monster of chaos (26:12; Isaiah 51:9), not the Rahab of Jericho, who is spelled differently in Hebrew.

  • v17 "with a tempest" — bi-se'arah; with other vowels, bi-sa'arah, for a hair, for a trifle. Without cause is chinnam, as in 1:9 and 2:3, though Job does not know it.

  • v19 "who will summon me?" — the Hebrew has me; the Greek reads the line of God, who will stand against His judgment? Job may be quoting God's answer: who will summon Me?

  • v26 "ships of reed" — light papyrus boats of the Nile (Isaiah 18:2).

  • v31 "into a pit" — shachat, a muddy pit; even after washing in snow and lye he would come out filthier than his clothes could bear.

  • v33 "There is no arbiter between us" — mokhiach, one who decides between two parties and can lay a hand on both; the Greek reads Would that there were an arbiter between us. Job's longing for a go-between returns in 16:19–21 and 19:25.

chapters.title: Your Hands Shaped Me
chapters.html:
Job 10

Why Do You Contend with Me?

1My soul is weary of my life;
I will give free rein to my complaint;
I will speak in the bitterness of my soul.

2I will say to God, Do not condemn me;
let me know why You contend against me.

3Does it seem good to You to oppress,
to despise the work of Your hands
and shine on the counsel of the wicked?

4Do You have eyes of flesh?
Do You see as man sees?

5Are Your days like the days of man,
or Your years like a man's years,

6that You seek out my iniquity
and search for my sin,

7though You know that I am not guilty,
and there is no one to deliver out of Your hand?

You Made Me like Clay

8Your hands shaped me and made me,
all of me, all around, and now You swallow me up.

9Remember that You made me like clay;
will You return me to dust?

10Did You not pour me out like milk
and curdle me like cheese?

11You clothed me with skin and flesh
and knit me together with bones and sinews.

12Life and loyal love You have granted me,
and Your care has kept my spirit.

13Yet these things You hid in Your heart;
I know that this was in Your mind:

14if I sinned, You would watch me
and not acquit me of my iniquity.

15If I am guilty, woe to me!
If I am in the right, I cannot lift up my head,
filled with disgrace and looking on my affliction.

16Should it lift itself up, You hunt me like a lion,
and again show Your wonders against me.

17You renew Your witnesses against me
and increase Your anger toward me;
fresh troops and a host are against me.

Leave Me Alone

18Why did You bring me out from the womb?
I should have breathed my last, and no eye would have seen me.

19I would have been as though I had not been,
carried from the belly to the grave.

20Are not my days few? Cease,

21before I go, never to return,
to the land of darkness and deep shadow,

22a land of gloom like thick darkness,
of deep shadow without order,
where the light is like thick darkness.

Notes

  • v3 "the work of Your hands" — the theme of the chapter: God made Job with care (vv8–12), and now seems bent on destroying what He made.

  • vv4–5 "eyes of flesh… the days of man" — Job asks whether God, like a human judge with little time and poor sight, must torture a confession out of him.

  • vv10–11 "pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese… knit me together" — the forming of a child in the womb; You knitted me together in my mother's womb (Psalm 139:13).

  • v12 "loyal love" — chesed, as in Ruth 1:8. Your care, pequddatekha, is God's watching over him, the same root as visit in 7:18.

  • v16 "Should it lift itself up" — yig'eh, it rises: Job's head, from v15. God the lion-hunter, as in Hosea 13:7–8; earlier Job compared the wicked to lions (4:10–11).

  • v17 "fresh troops and a host" — chalifot ve-tsava, reliefs and an army, wave after wave of soldiers sent against him.

  • v18 "Why did You bring me out from the womb?" — the question of 3:11, now asked of God directly.

  • v20 "Cease, and leave me alone" — the written text has Let Him cease… let Him set; the read form, followed here, speaks to God directly. The Greek has Let me alone, that I may rest a little.

  • vv21–22 "the land of darkness" — Sheol, described with every Hebrew word for darkness; in it even the light is like thick darkness.

chapters.title: Zophar Speaks
chapters.html:
Job 11

1Zophar the Naamathite answered and said:

Oh That God Would Speak

2Shall a multitude of words go unanswered,
and a man full of talk be judged right?

3Should your babble silence men,
and when you mock, shall no one put you to shame?

4For you say, "My teaching is pure,
and I am clean in Your eyes."

5But oh that God would speak
and open His lips against you,

6and tell you the secrets of wisdom!
For sound wisdom has two sides.
Know then that God exacts of you less than your iniquity deserves.

7Can you find out the deep things of God?
Can you find out the limit of the Almighty?

8It is as high as the heavens; what can you do?
Deeper than Sheol; what can you know?

9Its measure is longer than the earth
and broader than the sea.

10If He passes through and imprisons,
and calls the court together, who can turn Him back?

11For He knows worthless men;
He sees iniquity without needing to look into it.

12But a hollow man will get understanding
when a wild donkey's colt is born a man.

If You Set Your Heart Aright

13If you set your heart aright
and stretch out your hands toward Him,

14if iniquity is in your hand, put it far away,
and let no injustice dwell in your tents.

15Surely then you will lift up your face without blemish;
you will be firmly set and will not fear.

16You will forget your misery;
you will remember it as waters that have passed away.

17Your life will rise brighter than noonday;
its darkness will be like the morning.

18You will trust, because there is hope;
you will look around and lie down in safety.

19You will lie down, and no one will make you afraid;
many will seek your favor.

20But the eyes of the wicked will fail;
all way of escape will be lost to them,
and their hope is to breathe their last.

Notes

  • v1 Zophar — the third friend, and the bluntest. He is the only one of the three who speaks only twice; he has no speech in the third round (chapters 22–27).

  • v4 "My teaching is pure" — leqach, instruction, a word of the wisdom schools (Proverbs 4:2). Zophar sums up Job's claims more sharply than Job made them.

  • v6 "sound wisdom has two sides" — kiflayim, double: what is hidden of God's wisdom is as great again as what can be seen.

  • v6 "God exacts of you less than your iniquity deserves" — yashsheh lekha mi-avonekha, He causes some of your iniquity to be forgotten for you: Job is suffering less than he has earned. It is the harshest word any of the friends has yet spoken.

  • vv7–9 "the deep things of God… higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol" — Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! (Romans 11:33). God will speak of these dimensions Himself in 38:4–18.

  • v11 "without needing to look into it" — ve-lo yitbonan, and does not consider; read as a question, will He not consider it?

  • v12 "when a wild donkey's colt is born a man" — a proverb of what will never happen.

  • v15 "without blemish" — mi-mum, the word for a blemish on an offering (Leviticus 22:20); the face of a man with nothing to hide.

  • v20 "their hope is to breathe their last" — mappach nefesh, a breathing out of the soul: the only thing left for them to look forward to is death, as Job himself has hoped (6:8–9).

chapters.title: Ask the Beasts
chapters.html:
Job 12

1Job answered and said:

A Laughingstock to My Friends

2No doubt you are the people,
and wisdom will die with you.

3But I have understanding as well as you;
I am not inferior to you.
Who does not know such things as these?

4I am a laughingstock to my friends,
I who called to God and He answered me,
a laughingstock, the righteous and blameless man.

5In the thought of one at ease there is contempt for misfortune;
it is ready for those whose feet slip.

6The tents of robbers are at peace,
and those who provoke God are secure,
those who carry their god in their hand.

The Hand of the LORD Has Done This

7But ask the beasts, and they will teach you,
the birds of the heavens, and they will tell you;

8or speak to the earth, and it will teach you,
and the fish of the sea will declare it to you.

9Who among all these does not know
that the hand of the LORD has done this?

10In His hand is the life of every living thing
and the breath of all mankind.

11Does not the ear test words
as the palate tastes its food?

12Wisdom is with the aged,
and understanding in length of days.

13With Him are wisdom and might;
He has counsel and understanding.

14If He tears down, it will not be rebuilt;
if He shuts a man in, he will not be let out.

15If He holds back the waters, they dry up;
if He sends them out, they overturn the land.

16With Him are strength and sound wisdom;
the one led astray and the one who leads astray are His.

17He leads counselors away stripped,
and makes fools of judges.

18He loosens the bonds of kings
and binds a waistcloth on their hips.

19He leads priests away stripped
and overthrows the long established.

20He takes away the speech of those who are trusted
and removes the discernment of the elders.

21He pours contempt on nobles
and loosens the belt of the strong.

22He uncovers the deeps out of darkness
and brings deep shadow to light.

23He makes nations great, and He destroys them;
He spreads nations out, and He leads them away.

24He takes away the understanding of the chiefs of the people of the earth
and makes them wander in a trackless waste.

25They grope in the dark without light,
and He makes them stagger like a drunken man.

Notes

  • v2 "No doubt you are the people, and wisdom will die with you" — Job's sarcasm: the friends talk as if all wisdom were theirs alone.

  • v4 "the righteous and blameless man" — tsaddiq tamim, the man God answered, now mocked; tamim is the fuller form of tam (1:1).

  • v5 "contempt for misfortune" — lappid buz, which the old translations read as a torch despised; most now read le-fid, for disaster. The line is hard either way.

  • v6 "those who carry their god in their hand" — the sense is uncertain: those whose only god is their own strong hand (Habakkuk 1:11), or those who carry an idol.

  • v9 "the hand of the LORD has done this" — the only place in the speeches of Job and his friends (chapters 3–37) where the name YHWH appears. The line is word for word Isaiah 41:20.

  • v12 "Wisdom is with the aged" — taken by most as Job quoting the friends' boast (8:8–10), to answer it in v13: wisdom is with Him.

  • v14 "if He shuts a man in" — the hedge of 3:23 again.

  • v16 "the one led astray and the one who leads astray are His" — both the deceived and the deceiver are under His power.

  • vv17–25 — a hymn of God overturning the great: counselors, judges, kings, priests, elders, nations. Lines of it return in Psalm 107:40, He pours contempt on princes and makes them wander in trackless wastes.

  • v24 "a trackless waste" — tohu, the word of Genesis 1:2, without form, the world before God ordered it.

chapters.title: Though He Slay Me
chapters.html:
Job 13

Worthless Physicians

1My eye has seen all this;
my ear has heard and understood it.

2What you know, I also know;
I am not inferior to you.

3But I would speak to the Almighty,
and I desire to argue my case with God.

4As for you, you smear over with lies;
worthless physicians are you all.

5Oh that you would keep silent,
and it would be your wisdom!

6Hear now my argument,
and listen to the pleadings of my lips.

7Will you speak falsely for God
and speak deceitfully for Him?

8Will you show partiality toward Him?
Will you plead the case for God?

9Will it be well with you when He searches you out?
Or can you deceive Him, as one deceives a man?

10He will surely rebuke you
if in secret you show partiality.

11Will not His majesty terrify you,
and the dread of Him fall on you?

12Your maxims are proverbs of ashes;
your defenses are defenses of clay.

I Will Argue My Ways to His Face

13Be silent before me, and let me speak,
and let come on me what may.

14Why should I take my flesh in my teeth
and put my life in my hand?

15Though He slay me, I will hope in Him;
yet I will argue my ways to His face.

16This too will be my salvation,
that the godless will not come before Him.

17Listen closely to my words,
and let my declaration be in your ears.

18I have set my case in order;
I know that I will be in the right.

19Who is there who will contend with me?
For then I would be silent and breathe my last.

20Only two things do not do to me,
then I will not hide myself from Your face:

21take Your hand far from me,
and let not dread of You terrify me.

22Then call, and I will answer;
or let me speak, and You reply to me.

23How many are my iniquities and my sins?
Make me know my transgression and my sin.

24Why do You hide Your face
and count me as Your enemy?

25Will You frighten a driven leaf
and pursue dry chaff?

26For You write bitter things against me
and make me inherit the iniquities of my youth.

27You put my feet in the stocks
and watch all my paths;
You mark a line around the soles of my feet.

28He wastes away like a rotten thing,
like a garment that the moth has eaten.

Notes

  • v4 "you smear over with lies… worthless physicians" — tofelei sheqer, plasterers of falsehood, who cover the crack instead of mending it (Ezekiel 13:10–12); rofe'ei elil, healers of nothing.

  • v8 "Will you show partiality toward Him?" — ha-panav tissa'un, will you lift His face, the phrase for favoring one side in court (Leviticus 19:15). Job warns that God Himself hates a false witness, even one on His own side.

  • v12 "proverbs of ashes… defenses of clay" — sayings that crumble, and shields (gabbim, bosses, mounds) made of mud.

  • v14 "take my flesh in my teeth and put my life in my hand" — two sayings for risking one's life (1 Samuel 19:5; 28:21).

  • v15 "Though He slay me, I will hope in Him" — the written text has lo, not: He will slay me; I have no hope; the read form, followed here, has lo, in Him. The two are opposite in sense; both are old. The second line holds either way: Job will argue his case to God's face.

  • v16 "the godless will not come before Him" — Job's daring to appear before God is itself the proof that he is not godless (chanef, the word Bildad used of him in 8:13).

  • v18 "I have set my case in order" — arakhti mishpat, the words of a man who has drawn up his case for court (23:4).

  • v24 "count me as Your enemy" — oyev, enemy, sounds like Iyyov, Job, and the rabbis drew the link: God treats Job as His foe.

  • v27 "You mark a line around the soles of my feet" — titchaqqeh, You carve: a mark cut on a slave's or prisoner's feet, or a line he may not cross.

  • v28 "He wastes away" — he, man; the line leads into the next chapter, Man who is born of a woman (14:1).

chapters.title: If a Man Dies
chapters.html:
Job 14

Few of Days

1Man who is born of a woman
is few of days and full of trouble.

2He comes out like a flower and withers;
he flees like a shadow and does not stay.

3Do You open Your eyes on such a one,
and bring me into judgment with You?

4Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?
Not one.

5Since his days are determined,
the number of his months is with You,
and You have set his limits that he cannot pass,

6look away from him and let him rest,
till he can enjoy his day like a hired worker.

Hope for a Tree

7For there is hope for a tree:
if it is cut down, it will sprout again,
and its shoots will not cease.

8Though its root grows old in the earth,
and its stump dies in the dust,

9at the scent of water it will bud
and put out branches like a young plant.

10But a man dies and lies powerless;
man breathes his last, and where is he?

11As waters vanish from the sea,
and a river wastes away and dries up,

12so a man lies down and does not rise;
till the heavens are no more they will not awake,
nor be roused out of their sleep.

Will He Live Again?

13Oh that You would hide me in Sheol,
that You would conceal me until Your anger turns back,
that You would set me a time, and remember me!

14If a man dies, will he live again?
All the days of my service I would wait,
till my relief should come.

15You would call, and I would answer You;
You would long for the work of Your hands.

16For then You would number my steps;
You would not keep watch over my sin.

17My transgression would be sealed up in a bag,
and You would cover over my iniquity.

18But as a mountain falls and crumbles away,
and a rock is moved from its place,

19as the waters wear away the stones
and their torrents wash away the soil of the earth,
so You destroy the hope of man.

20You overpower him forever, and he goes;
You change his face and send him away.

21His sons come to honor, and he does not know it;
they are brought low, and he does not perceive it.

22He feels only the pain of his own flesh,
and mourns only for himself.

Notes

  • v1 "Man who is born of a woman" — the line Eliphaz throws back at Job in 15:14. Trouble is rogez, the turmoil of 3:17 and 3:26.

  • v4 "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one." — the shortest verse in the book's poetry; the Hebrew is two lines of three words and two. Surely I was brought forth in iniquity (Psalm 51:5).

  • v6 "like a hired worker" — the image of 7:1–2: let man have at least the hired man's evening rest.

  • vv7–9 "there is hope for a tree" — a cut tree sprouts again from the stump (Isaiah 11:1); hope, tiqvah, is what Job finds in the tree and not in man.

  • v12 "till the heavens are no more" — that is, never; yet the heavens will vanish like smoke (Isaiah 51:6), and the line has been read in the light of the resurrection.

  • v14 "If a man dies, will he live again?" — the question at the center of the chapter. My relief is chalifati, the word of the fresh troops of 10:17: the soldier's term of service (7:1) ends when the relief arrives.

  • v15 "You would long for the work of Your hands" — the plea of 10:3 and 10:8 turned to hope: God will want back what He made.

  • v16 "For then You would number my steps" — ki attah, which can also mean for now; read so, the verse is a complaint, like 13:27, and not a hope.

  • v17 "sealed up in a bag" — like a purse tied and sealed, put away and not opened again (Hosea 13:12).

  • vv18–19 — the mountain, the rock and the soil are worn down slowly; so the hope of v7–15 is worn away.

chapters.title: Eliphaz's Second Speech
chapters.html:
Job 15

1Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:

Your Own Mouth Condemns You

2Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge,
and fill his belly with the east wind?

3Should he argue with talk that does no good,
or with words that are of no use?

4But you are doing away with the fear of God
and cutting short devotion before God.

5For your iniquity teaches your mouth,
and you choose the tongue of the crafty.

6Your own mouth condemns you, and not I;
your own lips testify against you.

7Were you the first man to be born?
Were you brought forth before the hills?

8Have you listened in the council of God?
Do you keep wisdom to yourself?

9What do you know that we do not know?
What do you understand that is not with us?

10Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us,
older than your father.

11Are the comforts of God too small for you,
or the word spoken gently with you?

12Why does your heart carry you away,
and why do your eyes flash,

13that you turn your spirit against God
and bring such words out of your mouth?

14What is man, that he can be pure,
or one born of a woman, that he can be righteous?

15He puts no trust in His holy ones,
and the heavens are not clean in His sight;

16how much less one who is detestable and corrupt,
a man who drinks injustice like water!

The Fate of the Wicked

17I will show you; hear me,
and what I have seen I will declare,

18what wise men have told,
and did not hide from their fathers,

19to whom alone the land was given,
and no stranger passed among them.

20The wicked man writhes in pain all his days,
all the number of years laid up for the ruthless.

21A sound of terrors is in his ears;
in time of peace the destroyer will come on him.

22He does not believe that he will return out of darkness,
and he is marked out for the sword.

23He wanders about for bread: "Where is it?"
He knows that a day of darkness is ready at his hand.

24Distress and anguish terrify him;
they overpower him, like a king ready for the attack.

25For he has stretched out his hand against God
and plays the mighty man against the Almighty,

26running at Him with neck outstretched,
behind the thick bosses of his shields.

27For he has covered his face with his fat
and put layers of fat on his loins,

28and has lived in ruined cities,
in houses no one should live in,
marked out to become heaps of rubble.

29He will not be rich, and his wealth will not last,
and his gains will not bend down to the earth.

30He will not escape from darkness;
the flame will dry up his shoots,
and he will depart by the breath of His mouth.

31Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself,
for emptiness will be his reward.

32It will be paid in full before his day,
and his branch will not be green.

33He will shake off his unripe grapes like the vine,
and cast off his blossom like the olive tree.

34For the company of the godless is barren,
and fire consumes the tents of bribery.

35They conceive trouble and give birth to iniquity,
and their womb prepares deceit.

Notes

  • v2 "the east wind" — the hot desert wind, qadim; Job's words are hot air (8:2).

  • v4 "cutting short devotion before God" — sichah, meditation, complaint: by his talk Job undermines the reverence that others owe to God.

  • v7 "Were you the first man to be born? Were you brought forth before the hills?" — words of Wisdom in Proverbs 8:25, before the hills, I was brought forth. Eliphaz mocks Job as though he claimed to be older than creation.

  • v8 "the council of God" — sod Eloah, the heavenly council of 1:6, where the LORD's secret counsel is spoken (Jeremiah 23:18).

  • v11 "the comforts of God" — Eliphaz counts his own speeches as God's comfort, spoken gently; compare 4:2.

  • vv14–16 — Eliphaz repeats the night voice of 4:17–19, now with Job's own words of 14:1, born of a woman. Detestable is nit'av, from the root of to'evah.

  • v19 "no stranger passed among them" — the wisdom Eliphaz offers is old and pure, untouched by foreign teaching.

  • v24 "like a king ready for the attack" — kidor, a word found only here, perhaps onset, battle.

  • v29 "his gains will not bend down to the earth" — minlam, a word found only here; perhaps his crops or his possessions, too thin to bow under their own weight.

  • v33 "like the vine… like the olive tree" — a vine dropping its grapes before they ripen, an olive shedding its blossom: a life that bears nothing.

chapters.title: My Witness Is in Heaven
chapters.html:
Job 16

1Job answered and said:

Miserable Comforters

2I have heard many such things;
miserable comforters are you all.

3Is there an end to windy words?
Or what provokes you, that you answer?

4I too could speak as you do,
if you were in my place;
I could string words together against you
and shake my head at you.

5I could strengthen you with my mouth,
and the comfort of my lips would ease your pain.

6If I speak, my pain is not eased,
and if I hold back, how much of it leaves me?

He Set Me Up as His Target

7But now He has worn me out;
You have made desolate all my company.

8You have shriveled me up, and it has become a witness;
my leanness has risen up against me; it testifies to my face.

9His anger has torn me, and He has hated me;
He has gnashed His teeth at me;
my adversary sharpens his eyes against me.

10They have gaped at me with their mouth;
they have struck my cheek in scorn;
they mass themselves together against me.

11God hands me over to the unjust
and throws me into the hands of the wicked.

12I was at ease, and He broke me apart;
He seized me by the neck and shattered me;
He set me up as His target.

13His archers surround me;
He slashes open my kidneys and does not spare;
He pours out my gall on the ground.

14He breaks me with breach on breach;
He runs at me like a warrior.

15I have sewn sackcloth on my skin
and laid my horn in the dust.

16My face is red with weeping,
and on my eyelids is deep shadow,

17although there is no violence in my hands,
and my prayer is pure.

O Earth, Do Not Cover My Blood

18O earth, do not cover my blood,
and let my cry find no resting place.

19Even now, my witness is in heaven,
and the one who testifies for me is on high.

20My friends scorn me;
my eye pours out tears to God,

21that he would argue the case of a man with God,
as a son of man does for his friend.

22For when a few years have come,
I will go the way from which I will not return.

Notes

  • v2 "miserable comforters" — menachamei amal, comforters of trouble, who bring trouble instead of comfort; the friends came to comfort him (2:11).

  • v4 "shake my head at you" — the gesture of scorn, all who see me mock me… they wag their heads (Psalm 22:7).

  • v7 "He has worn me out; You have made desolate" — Job moves from speaking of God to speaking to Him and back, in one line; the Hebrew does the same.

  • v9 "my adversary sharpens his eyes against me" — God pictured as a beast of prey and as an enemy in battle. Adversary is tsar, not the satan of chapters 1–2; Job does not know of the scene in heaven.

  • v10 "they have struck my cheek in scorn" — I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard (Isaiah 50:6; Lamentations 3:30).

  • v15 "laid my horn in the dust" — the horn is a man's strength and honor (1 Samuel 2:1; Psalm 75:10).

  • v18 "O earth, do not cover my blood" — blood that the earth does not cover goes on crying out for justice, as Abel's did (Genesis 4:10; Isaiah 26:21).

  • v19 "my witness is in heaven" — sahadi, an Aramaic word, my testifier. Job has said there is no arbiter (9:33); now he looks for one in heaven, and in 19:25 he names his redeemer.

  • v20 "My friends scorn me" — melitsai re'ai; melits can also be interpreter, advocate, as in 33:23, so the line can be read my advocate is my friend.

  • v21 "as a son of man does for his friend" — ben adam, the same phrase as in Psalm 8:4 and 80:17.

chapters.title: Where Then Is My Hope?
chapters.html:
Job 17

My Spirit Is Broken

1My spirit is broken; my days are snuffed out;
the graves are ready for me.

2Surely there are mockers around me,
and my eye dwells on their provocation.

3Lay down a pledge for me with Yourself;
who else will strike hands with me?

4Since You have closed their hearts to understanding,
therefore You will not let them triumph.

5One who informs against his friends for a share of their goods,
the eyes of his children will fail.

6He has made me a byword of the peoples,
and I am one in whose face they spit.

7My eye has grown dim from grief,
and all my limbs are like a shadow.

8The upright are appalled at this,
and the innocent stirs himself up against the godless.

9Yet the righteous holds to his way,
and the one who has clean hands grows stronger and stronger.

Where Then Is My Hope?

10But you, come back, all of you, and come on;
I will not find a wise man among you.

11My days are past; my plans are broken off,
the desires of my heart.

12They make night into day:
"The light is near," in the face of darkness.

13If I hope for Sheol as my house,
if I spread out my bed in darkness,

14if I say to the pit, "You are my father,"
and to the worm, "My mother," and "My sister,"

15where then is my hope?
Who will see my hope?

16Will it go down to the bars of Sheol?
Shall we go down together into the dust?

Notes

  • v1 "my days are snuffed out" — niz'akhu, a word found only here, as a lamp goes out.

  • v3 "Lay down a pledge for me with Yourself… strike hands" — the gesture of standing surety for another's debt (Proverbs 6:1; 17:18). Job asks God to stand surety for him against God; no one else will.

  • v5 — the sense of the line is uncertain. It reads like a proverb: one who betrays his friends for gain brings ruin on his own children. Job may be quoting it against the friends.

  • v6 "one in whose face they spit" — tofet, spitting; not the Topheth of the valley of Hinnom, which is spelled the same.

  • v8 "the innocent stirs himself up against the godless" — likely Job turning the friends' words against them: they claim to be the upright, appalled at him.

  • v10 "I will not find a wise man among you" — the answer to Eliphaz's claim of 15:9–10 that the wise are on the friends' side.

  • v12 "They make night into day" — the friends promise light (11:17) when darkness is upon him.

  • vv13–14 "to the pit, 'You are my father'… to the worm, 'My mother'" — the grave as his family home; the worm is spread out beneath you (Isaiah 14:11). The pit is shachat, as in 9:31.

  • vv15–16 "where then is my hope?… the bars of Sheol" — the gates of the underworld, closed behind those who enter (Jonah 2:6). The Greek reads, Will they go down with me to Hades?, of Job's hopes.
